## The question

F05 asked which arm a subject belongs to. That treats adaptation as two boxes,
which throws away information: a subject just over the HR threshold and one far
above it are not the same.

This asks the continuous version. Given a subject's proteome, can we forecast
*how much* muscle they gain? Same cross-validation discipline, different
outcome and a different score.

## The outcomes

```{r}
#| label: outcomes
#| echo: false
tibble::tibble(
  outcome = ADAPT_OUTCOMES,
  what = c(
    "composite hypertrophy score",
    "change in type I fibre cross-sectional area",
    "change in type II fibre cross-sectional area",
    "change in whole-muscle cross-sectional area",
    "change in leg-press one-rep max",
    "change in knee-extension one-rep max"
  )
)
```

Six outcomes rather than one, because "adaptation" is not a single measurement.
Fibre-level and whole-muscle-level change need not agree, and strength need not
track size. Each is predicted separately, and the outcome axis is part of the
screen size.

## Scoring a continuous forecast

### The idea

The obvious score is $R^2$, but $R^2$ computed on the same data a model was
fitted to always rises when you add features and cannot go below zero. Out of
sample neither is true.

$Q^2$ is the out-of-sample version. It compares the model's squared error to the
error you would make by ignoring the proteome entirely and predicting every
subject's outcome as the group mean. $Q^2 = 1$ is perfect. $Q^2 = 0$ means the
model is exactly as good as guessing the mean. **$Q^2 < 0$ means it is worse
than guessing the mean**, which is possible out of sample and common at $n=16$.

### Formally

$$
Q^2 = 1 - \frac{\mathrm{PRESS}}{\mathrm{TSS}}
= 1 - \frac{\sum_{s}\big(y_s - \hat{y}_{-s}\big)^2}{\sum_{s}\big(y_s - \bar{y}\big)^2}
$$

$\hat{y}_{-s}$ is the prediction for subject $s$ from a model fitted without
them, so PRESS is a genuine prediction error. Nothing here is in-sample.

Spearman correlation between observed and predicted is reported beside it. The
two can disagree: a model can rank subjects correctly while being badly
calibrated in magnitude, giving positive $\rho$ and negative $Q^2$. When they
disagree, $Q^2$ is the one that answers "is this a forecast".

## Everything else carries over from F05

The cross-validation, the nesting, the leakage discipline and the permutation
null are identical to F05 and are explained there. Two differences:

- The permutation shuffles the **outcome value** across subjects rather than a
  binary label.
- The trivial baseline is $Q^2 > 0$, not AUC $> 0.5$.

```{r}
#| label: lead-def
LEAD_BASELINE
```

The below-baseline trap bites harder here. A discrete permutation null can flag
a $Q^2$ of $-0.02$ as unusual, and without the baseline condition that cell
would be counted as a lead — a model that predicts worse than the mean, promoted
for being unusually bad.

## The screen

```{r}
#| label: grid
#| echo: false
tibble::tibble(
  axis = c("feature level", "timepoint config", "model", "outcome"),
  n = c(
    length(SWEEP_LEVELS), length(SWEEP_CONFIGS),
    length(CONT_METHODS) + 1L, length(ADAPT_OUTCOMES)
  ),
  values = c(
    paste(SWEEP_LEVELS, collapse = ", "),
    paste(SWEEP_CONFIGS, collapse = ", "),
    paste(c(CONT_METHODS, PLAIN_METHOD), collapse = ", "),
    paste(ADAPT_OUTCOMES, collapse = ", ")
  )
)
```

792 cells. The outcome axis multiplies the screen by six relative to F05, which
is exactly why the screen size has to travel with every number reported from it.

## The figure

![F06 prediction composite](../b_reports/F06_prediction_composite.png)

- **A** The twelve cells with the smallest permutation $p$, each observed against
  predicted, points coloured by responder arm, fit line keyed to feature level,
  $Q^2$ and its permutation $p$ printed per cell.
- **B** The specification curve: all cells sorted by $Q^2$ against their null
  bands, with a strip reading off level, config, method and outcome.

In panel A, look at the spread of the points before the line. A high $Q^2$
driven by two extreme subjects at opposite corners is not a forecast; it is a
two-point fit with fourteen subjects in a cloud between them.

## The result

```{r}
#| label: result
#| echo: false
cells <- read.xlsx(
  here("05_Figures", "F06_prediction", "c_data", "results.xlsx"), "all_cells"
) |>
  best_b_per_cell()

has_null <- any(!is.na(cells$perm_p_q2))

cells |>
  summarise(
    cells = dplyr::n(),
    median_q2 = round(median(.data$q2, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    max_q2 = round(max(.data$q2, na.rm = TRUE), 3),
    above_zero = sum(.data$q2 > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    leads = if (has_null) {
      sum(is_lead(.data$q2, .data$perm_p_q2, "cont"), na.rm = TRUE)
    } else {
      NA_integer_
    },
    .by = "level"
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: null-status
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
if (has_null) {
  cat("Permutation nulls are present, so the lead column is interpretable.\n")
} else {
  cat(
    "**Permutation nulls are not in this run.** The sweep was executed at",
    "B = 0 to get point estimates quickly; `leads` is therefore undefined and",
    "no cell can be called significant. The B = 200 pass fills it in.\n"
  )
}
```

The median $Q^2$ is the number to sit with. Across the whole screen it is
negative — the typical cell predicts worse than the outcome's own mean. Cells
above zero exist, and the maximum is well above zero, but that is what a maximum
over hundreds of draws does.

## How to read this honestly

Three cautions travel with any lead from this screen.

**The screen size.** 792 cells at a 5% chance rate yields about 40 cells below
$p<.05$ with no signal at all. A count of leads only means something against
that denominator, which is why F07 plots every best cell against its own null
and prints the number of cells it was drawn from.

**Imputation.** Every cell runs on the missForest-imputed proteome, imputed once
across the cohort rather than inside each fold. An earlier experiment on this
project showed a module-to-ΔmCSA result collapsing entirely once imputation and
module definition moved in-fold. The same optimism applies here in principle.

**Concentration is suggestive, not confirmatory.** If leads cluster on one
outcome across several levels, configs and methods, that is more interesting
than a single lucky cell — dependence across cells makes it weaker evidence than
it looks, but it is the pattern worth taking to a validation cohort.

## Recap

- $Q^2$ is out-of-sample $R^2$; below zero means worse than predicting the mean.
- Spearman and $Q^2$ can disagree; $Q^2$ answers "is this a forecast".
- The baseline condition stops a below-chance cell being promoted by a discrete
  null.
- 792 cells, so roughly 40 would clear $p<.05$ by luck alone.
- Any lead is a hypothesis for a validation cohort, not a predictor.
